goals: Explain why many Italians were discontented after the First World War
Describe the economic and political conditions that weakened Italy
Explain how Mussolini came to power in 1922

slides.heading: Why did democracy fail in Italy?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the causes of **Fascism** and **Mussolini's** rise to power.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: Italy after the war, the mutilated victory, economic crisis, weak governments, fear of communism, and the March on Rome in 1922
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: After the First World War, democracy collapsed in several European countries and dictators took power. The first was Italy. In this part we look at why many Italians were angry after the war, why their governments were weak, and how Benito Mussolini and his Fascist Party came to power in nineteen twenty-two.

slides.narration: This timeline covers both dictatorships. Mussolini started the fascist movement in nineteen nineteen and came to power in nineteen twenty-two. Germany suffered hyperinflation in nineteen twenty-three and the Depression from nineteen twenty-nine. Hitler became Chancellor in nineteen thirty-three and Führer in nineteen thirty-four.

slides.heading: Italy after the war
slides.body_md: A **winner** that felt like a **loser**.

rows: Italy joined the war in 1915 on the Allied side
Heavy losses of soldiers and money
Fiume and most of Dalmatia not given

visual.alt: Table of Italy after the First World War: it joined the Allies in 1915 expecting land, suffered heavy losses, was not given Fiume and most of Dalmatia in 1919, and nationalists spoke of a mutilated victory

slides.narration: Italy joined the war in nineteen fifteen on the side of Britain and France, hoping to gain territory. It lost many soldiers and spent huge sums. At the peace conference of nineteen nineteen, however, it did not receive all it had hoped for. Many Italians felt their sacrifice had been wasted.

slides.heading: Quick check: the country
slides.body_md: In which country did Mussolini lead the Fascist Party?
slides.narration: Begin with the basics. Which country did Mussolini lead?

slides.heading: A "mutilated victory"
slides.body_md: **Fiume** and most of **Dalmatia** were not given to Italy.

rows: Felt ignored by the big powers

visual.alt: Table of the mutilated victory: Italians hoped for Dalmatia, Fiume and honour as a victor, but mostly did not receive them and felt ignored
visual.caption: Why many Italians felt cheated.

slides.narration: Italian nationalists expected land on the Adriatic coast, especially Dalmatia, and the port of Fiume. Neither was given to Italy in nineteen nineteen. They described the result as a mutilated victory and blamed their own government for accepting it. This anger became fuel for Mussolini.

slides.heading: Economic crisis
slides.body_md: **Unemployment**, rising **prices** and **war debts**.

rows: Wage earners and the middle class

visual.alt: Table of economic problems in Italy after 1918: unemployment of returning soldiers and workers, rising prices hurting wage earners and the middle class, war debts, and strikes and land seizures that alarmed owners

slides.narration: The war left Italy poor. Soldiers came home to find no jobs. Prices rose faster than wages, and the government carried heavy war debts. Workers struck for better pay, and in some areas peasants took over land. Hardship made many people ready to listen to anyone who promised a way out.

slides.heading: Weak governments
slides.body_md: **Coalitions** that came and went.

visual.alt: Flow of political weakness in Italy: no party had a majority, so short-lived coalitions followed one another, problems were left unsolved, people lost faith in parliament and wanted a strong leader
visual.caption: Weak governments, 1919–22.

slides.narration: In parliament no party had a majority, so governments were coalitions of several parties. They quarrelled and fell quickly. Between nineteen nineteen and nineteen twenty-two such governments could not solve unemployment or stop the strikes. Many Italians lost faith in parliament and began to want a strong leader instead.

slides.heading: Fear of communism and the fascist squads
slides.body_md: Strikes and occupations of **1919–20**; the **Blackshirts**.

visual.alt: Table of the fear of communism in Italy: strikes and factory occupations in 1919 and 1920 and land seizures alarmed owners; the fascist movement founded at Milan in 1919 used Blackshirt squads against socialists and was funded by owners

slides.narration: In nineteen nineteen and nineteen twenty, workers occupied factories and raised red flags, and peasants seized estates. Owners feared a revolution like the one in Russia. Mussolini had started the fascist movement at Milan in nineteen nineteen. His armed squads, the Blackshirts, attacked socialists, and many owners paid them.

slides.heading: The March on Rome, 1922
slides.body_md: Power by **threat**, not by a majority.

nodes.label: October 1922: fascist squads gather to march on Rome
King Victor Emmanuel III refuses to use the army
Mussolini invited to become Prime Minister

visual.alt: Flow of the March on Rome: in October 1922 fascist squads gathered to march on Rome, the government could not resist, King Victor Emmanuel III refused to use the army, and Mussolini was invited to become Prime Minister
visual.caption: Power without a majority.

slides.narration: In October nineteen twenty-two, thousands of Fascists gathered to march on Rome. The government wanted to use the army, but King Victor Emmanuel the Third refused. Instead he invited Mussolini to become Prime Minister. Mussolini came to power although his party had only a small number of seats in parliament.

slides.heading: Mussolini's leadership
slides.body_md: Order, greatness and **spectacle**.

rows: Strong action against strikes and communism

visual.alt: Table of how Mussolini won support: promising order against strikes and communism, talking of national greatness, using uniforms, parades and symbols, and the title Il Duce

slides.narration: Mussolini was a powerful speaker and a former journalist. He promised order, strong action against communism and a return to national greatness. Uniforms, parades and symbols attracted young people and former soldiers. He took the title Il Duce, meaning the leader, and later turned Italy into a one-party state.

slides.narration: To sum up Part One. Italians felt cheated by a mutilated victory. Unemployment, rising prices and debts brought hardship. Weak coalition governments could not cope, and fear of communism drove owners to back Mussolini's Blackshirts. After the March on Rome in nineteen twenty-two, the King invited Mussolini to become Prime Minister.

decks.title: Rise of Dictatorships — Part 2: Nazism in Germany and the Shared Ideas
goals: Explain the causes of the rise of Nazism in Germany
Describe how Hitler came to power and became a dictator
Compare the ideologies of Fascism and Nazism

slides.heading: How did Hitler come to power?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the causes of **Nazism**, Hitler's path to power, and what the two ideologies shared.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the Weimar Republic, resentment of Versailles, the crises of 1923 and 1929, Hitler in power in 1933, and the shared ideas of the dictatorships
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Germany had become a democratic republic after the war. Yet in nineteen thirty-three Adolf Hitler, leader of the Nazi Party, came to power and soon became a dictator. In this part we study the causes, the steps by which he took control, and the ideas that Nazism shared with Italian Fascism.

slides.heading: The Weimar Republic
slides.body_md: A democracy **born in defeat**.

rows: Linked by many Germans with the hated treaty
Communists and nationalists both attacked it

visual.alt: Table of the weaknesses of the Weimar Republic: born in defeat in 1919 and linked with the treaty, many parties and unstable coalitions, Article 48 allowing rule by decree, and enemies on the left and right

slides.narration: The new German republic was set up in nineteen nineteen and is called the Weimar Republic. Many Germans linked it with defeat and the hated peace treaty. Proportional voting produced many parties, so governments were unstable coalitions. Article forty-eight let the President rule by emergency decree, a power later misused.

slides.heading: Quick check: the republic
slides.body_md: What was the democratic German republic of 1919–33 commonly called?
slides.narration: What name do historians give to Germany's democratic republic after the war?

slides.heading: Resentment of Versailles
slides.body_md: **War guilt**, **reparations**, lost **land**.

nodes.label: Nazi promise to overturn the treaty

visual.alt: Flow from the Treaty of Versailles to Nazi support: the war-guilt clause, reparations, loss of land and colonies and the small army created a sense of humiliation, which the Nazis used by promising to overturn the treaty
visual.caption: Resentment the Nazis could use.

slides.narration: The Treaty of Versailles blamed Germany for the war, demanded reparations, took away land and colonies and cut its army to one hundred thousand men. Many Germans felt humiliated. The Nazis called the treaty a national disgrace and promised to overturn it, which won them support.

slides.heading: Hyperinflation, 1923
slides.body_md: Money became almost **worthless**.

rows: Ruhr occupied by France and Belgium; money printed

visual.alt: Table of the hyperinflation of 1923: the Ruhr was occupied by France and Belgium and money was printed, so money became almost worthless and middle-class savers and pensioners lost most

slides.narration: In nineteen twenty-three, after France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr industrial region, the German government printed huge amounts of money. Prices rose by the hour and the mark became almost worthless. Middle-class families lost their savings and pensions, and many never trusted the republic again.

slides.heading: Quick check: worthless money
slides.body_md: True or false: German money became almost worthless in 1923.
slides.narration: Recall the crisis of the early twenties. Is the statement true?

slides.heading: The Great Depression
slides.body_md: From **1929**: millions **unemployed**.

nodes.label: American loans to Germany called back
Nazi votes rise; largest party in 1932

visual.alt: Flow of the Great Depression in Germany: the crash of October 1929 in New York led to American loans being recalled, factories closed and millions lost jobs, governments ruled by decree, and Nazi votes rose until they were the largest party in 1932
visual.caption: From crash to crisis.

slides.narration: In October nineteen twenty-nine prices on the New York stock market crashed. American loans to Germany were called back, factories closed and millions of Germans lost their jobs. Governments could not agree and ruled by decree. Desperate voters turned to the Nazis, who in nineteen thirty-two became the largest party in the Reichstag.

slides.heading: From largest party to Chancellor
slides.body_md: **Appointed** on **30 January 1933**.

nodes.label: Other parties and trade unions banned
2 August 1934: Hindenburg dies; Hitler becomes Fuhrer

visual.alt: Flow of Hitler's path to power: in 1932 the Nazis were the largest party without a majority; on 30 January 1933 Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor; the Enabling Act followed in March 1933; other parties and trade unions were banned; on 2 August 1934 Hindenburg died and Hitler became Fuhrer
visual.caption: From Chancellor to dictator.

slides.narration: The Nazis were the largest party in nineteen thirty-two but never won a majority in a free election. Conservative politicians believed they could control Hitler and persuaded President Hindenburg to appoint him Chancellor on the thirtieth of January nineteen thirty-three. Within eighteen months he had made himself dictator.

slides.heading: The Enabling Act and the Führer
slides.body_md: From Chancellor to **dictator**.

rows: Government could make laws without the Reichstag
Offices of President and Chancellor combined

visual.alt: Table of how Hitler secured power: the Enabling Act of March 1933 let the government make laws without the Reichstag, parties were banned in 1933, free trade unions were abolished, and in August 1934 he combined the offices of President and Chancellor as Fuhrer

slides.narration: In March nineteen thirty-three the Enabling Act let Hitler's government make laws without parliament. Other parties were banned and free trade unions abolished, so Germany became a one-party state. When President Hindenburg died in August nineteen thirty-four, Hitler combined the offices of President and Chancellor and took the title Führer.

slides.narration: Fascism and Nazism shared many ideas. Both created one-party states and banned opposition. Both preached extreme nationalism, glorified war and built a cult of the leader. Both were bitterly anti-communist, controlled the press and organised the young. The main difference was Nazism's racial doctrine.

slides.heading: Shared ideas and the main difference
columns:
**Shared**

- Totalitarian **one-party** state
- **Extreme nationalism**; glorified **war**
- **Cult of the leader**
- **Anti-communism**; no free **press**; **youth** groups

**Different**

- Nazism: a **racial doctrine** and **antisemitism**, leading to persecution and the **Holocaust**
- Early Italian Fascism: the **state**, not race, at the centre
slides.narration: Compare the two lists. On the left are the features both dictatorships shared. On the right is the key difference. Nazism made race its central idea and persecuted Jews, and millions of Jews and others were later murdered in the Holocaust. Early Italian Fascism placed the state, rather than race, at the centre.

sections.heading: 1. Italy after the First World War
sections.body_md:
- Italy joined the **Allies** in **1915** and suffered heavy losses.
- **Mutilated victory:** at the peace of **1919** it did not get **Fiume** and most of **Dalmatia**; nationalists blamed the government.
- **Economic crisis:** unemployment of ex-soldiers, inflation, war debts.
- **Weak governments:** no majority party; coalitions rose and fell.

key_terms.definition_md: The feeling that Italy had won the war but lost the peace.
A government formed by several parties together.

sections.heading: 2. Fear of communism and Mussolini's rise
sections.body_md:
- **1919–20:** strikes, factory occupations and land seizures alarmed owners.
- **Fascist movement:** founded by **Mussolini** at **Milan** in **1919**; National Fascist Party from **1921**; armed **Blackshirt** squads.
- **Support:** landowners and industrialists funded the squads; ex-soldiers and the middle class joined.
- **March on Rome:** **October 1922**; **King Victor Emmanuel III** invited Mussolini to be **Prime Minister**.
- Title: **Il Duce** (the leader).

sections.heading: 3. Germany: the Weimar Republic and Versailles
sections.body_md:
- **Weimar Republic (1919):** linked with defeat; many parties; unstable **coalitions**.
- **Article 48:** emergency rule by decree, used heavily from **1930**.
- **Treaty of Versailles:** war guilt, reparations, loss of land and colonies, army of **100,000**; seen as humiliation.
- The **Nazis** promised to overturn it.

key_terms.definition_md: The emergency-decree power of the German President.

sections.heading: 4. Economic crises: 1923 and 1929
sections.body_md:
- **1923:** after the occupation of the **Ruhr**, the government printed money; **hyperinflation** destroyed savings.
- **1929:** the **Great Depression**; American loans withdrawn; **millions unemployed** by 1932.
- Desperate voters turned to extremes; the **Nazis** became the **largest party** in **1932**.

sections.heading: 5. Hitler takes power
sections.body_md:
- **30 January 1933:** **President Hindenburg** appointed Hitler **Chancellor**; the Nazis had no majority.
- **March 1933:** **Enabling Act**: laws without the **Reichstag**.
- **1933:** other parties banned; free trade unions abolished.
- **2 August 1934:** Hindenburg died; Hitler became **Führer**.

sections.heading: 6. Fascism and Nazism compared
sections.body_md:
- **Shared:** totalitarian **one-party** state; **extreme nationalism**; glorification of **war**; **cult of the leader**; **anti-communism**; suppression of opposition and **civil liberties**; **propaganda**; **youth** organisations.
- **Difference:** Nazism's **racial doctrine** and **antisemitism** (the **Nuremberg Laws** of **1935** took away the rights of Jews); persecution led to the **Holocaust**, in which millions of Jews and others were murdered. Early Italian Fascism placed the **state** at the centre.

key_terms.definition_md: A state that tries to control every part of life under one party.
Hostility to and persecution of Jews.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying Mussolini or Hitler **won a majority**: both were **appointed**.
- Mixing **1923** (hyperinflation) with **1929** (Depression).
- Calling the Blackshirts German (they were **Italian**; the Nazi stormtroopers wore brown).
- Listing **race** as a shared feature: it was **central to Nazism**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the 4-mark part often asks you to explain or evaluate.

cards.back_md: Italian feeling that the war was won but the peace lost.
Strikes and factory occupations of **1919–20** in Italy.
War guilt; reparations; lost land; army of 100,000.
One party controls every part of life.
Leader shown as all-wise and always right.
Glorified as a sign of national strength.
Trained the young in loyalty to the leader.
**1935**: took away the rights of German Jews.
Give shared features first, then the difference.

questions.stem_md: Many Italians after 1919 described their country's gains from the peace settlement as a "mutilated victory". What did they mean?

options.text_md: Italy had lost the war and been occupied
Italy had been on the winning side but felt it received far less territory than it had expected
Italy had gained every territory it claimed
Italy had refused to sign any peace treaty

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Italy had been on the winning side but felt it received far less territory than it had expected. Italy fought on the winning side from 1915 but did not receive all the lands it hoped for, such as Dalmatia and Fiume, so many felt cheated. Italy was not defeated or occupied.

questions.stem_md: Which two areas on the Adriatic coast did many Italian nationalists feel Italy had been wrongly denied in the peace settlement?

options.text_md: Alsace and Lorraine
Danzig and the Saar
Bosnia and Serbia
Fiume and Dalmatia

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Fiume and Dalmatia. Italian nationalists resented that Italy did not get Fiume and most of Dalmatia. Alsace-Lorraine, Danzig and the Saar concerned Germany; Bosnia and Serbia are in the Balkans.

questions.stem_md: What did the March on Rome of October 1922 lead to?

options.text_md: The King inviting Mussolini to form a government as Prime Minister
The election of Hitler as Chancellor
Italy leaving the League of Nations
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The King inviting Mussolini to form a government as Prime Minister. Faced with the threat of fascist squads marching on the capital, King Victor Emmanuel III invited Mussolini to become Prime Minister at the end of October 1922.

questions.stem_md: Which economic condition in Italy after the First World War helped the Fascists win support?

options.text_md: A long boom with full employment
Large gains of colonies with rich mines
Rising prices, unemployment and war debts
The end of all taxes after the war

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rising prices, unemployment and war debts. The war left Italy with debts, inflation and unemployment, especially among returning soldiers. Discontent made people listen to Mussolini's promises.

questions.stem_md: Why were Italian governments between 1919 and 1922 unable to deal firmly with the country's problems?

options.text_md: Italy had no parliament at that time
The army ruled the country directly
They were weak coalitions of several parties that changed often
The League of Nations governed Italy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** They were weak coalitions of several parties that changed often. No party had a majority, so short-lived coalition governments followed one another and could not act firmly. Italy had a parliament, and neither the army nor the League ruled it.

questions.stem_md: Why did many Italian landowners and factory owners support the Fascists in 1919–22?

options.text_md: They feared a socialist or communist revolution after waves of strikes and occupations
They wanted Italy to join the Soviet Union
They wished to give their land to peasants
They wanted to restore the Treaty of Versailles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They feared a socialist or communist revolution after waves of strikes and occupations. Strikes, factory occupations and peasant land seizures in 1919–20 alarmed the propertied classes, who saw the Fascists as a force against socialism and communism.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Turin factory owner saw workers occupy his plant in 1920. In 1921 he pays a fascist squad, although he finds their talk of national glory tiresome and has no interest in Fiume. A friend says: "He backs them because Italy was cheated at the peace." Which reply fits the details best?

options.text_md: The friend is right, because every Italian who supported the Fascists did so out of anger over Fiume and Dalmatia
The friend is right, because the occupation shows that Italy had been defeated and was being run by workers
The owner was reacting to the Great Depression, which had by 1920 closed most Italian factories
His own experience points to fear of a socialist revolution; the peace-settlement grievance explains other supporters, such as nationalist veterans

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** His own experience points to fear of a socialist revolution; the peace-settlement grievance explains other supporters, such as nationalist veterans. The owner's loss of control in the occupation, and his lack of interest in nationalist claims, show that fear of socialism and communism moved him; the "mutilated victory" moved others. The Depression began only in 1929, Italy was on the winning side, and not every supporter shared one motive.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined Italians in 1920. Marco is a returned soldier with no job who is bitter that Italy did not receive Fiume. Elena owns an estate where peasants have seized some fields. Which statement best matches why each might turn to the Fascists?

options.text_md: Marco: fear of a socialist revolution; Elena: economic hardship and the "mutilated victory"
Marco: economic hardship and the "mutilated victory"; Elena: fear of a socialist revolution
Both mainly because unemployment hurt landowners as well as soldiers
Both mainly because the Great Depression of 1929 had ruined them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Marco: economic hardship and the "mutilated victory"; Elena: fear of a socialist revolution. Marco's unemployment and his anger over Fiume are economic hardship and the mutilated victory; Elena's seized fields show the propertied classes' fear of socialism. The causes are not swapped, landowners were driven by fear of revolution more than by unemployment, and the Depression began in 1929.

questions.stem_md: An imagined report from 1921 says a group of men in black shirts broke up a socialist meeting in a Po valley town while the local police stood by. Which group is described?

options.text_md: Fascist squads (the Blackshirts) of Mussolini
The Brownshirts (SA) of the Nazi Party
The Red Army
A League of Nations peace force

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Fascist squads (the Blackshirts) of Mussolini. Mussolini's armed squads wore black shirts and attacked socialists; the weak response of the authorities helped them grow. The Brownshirts were German.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Italian landowner in 1921 gives money to a fascist squad after peasants seize part of his estate. What does this suggest about who helped the Fascists rise?

options.text_md: The Fascists were supported only by the peasants
Propertied groups who feared losing their land and factories helped fund and protect them
The Fascists rose without any outside help
Foreign powers alone created the Fascist Party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Propertied groups who feared losing their land and factories helped fund and protect them. Landowners and industrialists, afraid of socialism, gave money and protection to the Fascists. The other options ignore this support from propertied classes.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Many Italians felt angry with their government after the First World War, although Italy had been on the winning side.

**Reason (R):** Italy did not receive all the territories it had hoped for, such as Fiume and Dalmatia.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the disappointment over territory (a "mutilated victory") turned many Italians against the governments that had accepted the settlement.

questions.stem_md: Mussolini was called Il ___, meaning "the leader".
questions.solution_md: His title was Il Duce, the leader.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Mussolini became Prime Minister in 1922 because the Fascist Party had won a majority of seats in parliament.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The Fascists held only a small number of seats; Mussolini was appointed by the King after the March on Rome, as governments seemed too weak to resist.

questions.stem_md: State two economic difficulties of Italy after 1918 that helped Mussolini gain support.
questions.solution_md: Two economic difficulties.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Unemployment**, especially among soldiers returning from the front.
2. **Rising prices** and heavy **war debts**, which hit workers and the middle class and made people look for a strong leader.

questions.stem_md: Why did the peace settlement after the First World War make many Italians discontented? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Italy fought on the **winning side** and lost many soldiers, yet it did not get **Fiume** and most of **Dalmatia**.
2. Nationalists called the result a **mutilated victory** and blamed the government for accepting it.

questions.stem_md: How did the weakness of Italian governments in 1919–22 help the Fascists?
questions.solution_md: Two points.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Short-lived **coalition** governments could not solve **unemployment** or end **strikes**, so people lost faith in parliament.
2. They failed to stop **fascist violence**, and in 1922 the King chose **Mussolini** rather than resist.

questions.stem_md: Why did the March on Rome bring Mussolini to power although his party had few seats in parliament?
questions.solution_md: Threat and the King's decision.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Thousands of armed **Fascists** threatened the capital, and the weak **government** seemed unable to resist.
2. **King Victor Emmanuel III**, fearing disorder or civil war, invited **Mussolini** to form a government in **October 1922**.

questions.stem_md: Give three causes of the rise of Fascism in Italy, with one fact for each.
questions.solution_md: Three causes, each with a fact.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Discontent with the peace settlement:** Italy did not receive **Fiume** and **Dalmatia**, so people spoke of a mutilated victory.
2. **Economic crisis:** **unemployment**, rising **prices** and war **debts** caused hardship.
3. **Fear of communism:** **strikes** and **factory occupations** in 1919–20 made landowners and industrialists back **Mussolini**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the rise of Fascism in Italy.

(i) Explain why many Italians were disappointed with the peace settlement after the First World War. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the economic and political conditions in Italy between 1919 and 1922 that weakened the government. **[3]**
(iii) How did Mussolini come to power in 1922? Explain the role of the fear of communism. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Peace settlement; conditions; path to power with fear of communism.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Italy joined the war on the winning side in **1915** and lost many soldiers. At the peace conference it did not receive **Fiume** and most of **Dalmatia**, which nationalists had expected. Many felt cheated and called it a **mutilated victory**, blaming their own leaders.

(ii) The war left **unemployment**, rising **prices** and large **debts**. Returning soldiers found no work. In parliament no party had a majority, so weak **coalition** governments changed often and could not act firmly.

(iii) In **1919–20** workers went on **strike** and occupied factories, and peasants seized land. **Landowners** and **industrialists**, fearing a communist revolution, gave money to Mussolini's **Blackshirt** squads, who attacked socialists. In **October 1922** the Fascists began the **March on Rome**; **King Victor Emmanuel III**, unwilling to resist, invited **Mussolini** to become **Prime Minister**.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Fear of communism and support for squads

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about Mussolini's rise.

(i) State three facts about the founding and growth of the Fascist Party between 1919 and 1921. **[3]**
(ii) Explain three ways in which Mussolini's leadership attracted support. **[3]**
(iii) "Weak governments did as much as Mussolini to bring Fascism to power." Give two arguments for this view and two against it. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Founding facts; leadership; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Mussolini** started the fascist movement at **Milan** in **1919**. Its armed squads, the **Blackshirts**, attacked socialists. In **1921** it became the **National Fascist Party**.

(ii) He was a skilled **speaker** and journalist who promised **order** and national **greatness**. He offered strong action against **communism**, which pleased property owners. He used **parades**, uniforms and symbols to win the young and ex-soldiers.

(iii) **For:** coalition governments failed to solve **unemployment** and **strikes**, and they did not stop **fascist violence**; the **King** chose to appoint Mussolini rather than use the army. **Against:** Mussolini built a disciplined **movement** and won the backing of **landowners** and **industrialists**; his **propaganda** and the **March on Rome** were his own actions.

questions.stem_md: Which term of the Treaty of Versailles did the Nazis use most to stir up anger, by calling the treaty a national humiliation?

options.text_md: The founding of the United Nations
The return of Fiume to Italy
The war-guilt clause that blamed Germany for the war
The creation of the Weimar constitution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The war-guilt clause that blamed Germany for the war. The war-guilt clause, with reparations and lost land, made many Germans feel humiliated; the Nazis promised to overturn the treaty. The United Nations came in 1945.

questions.stem_md: The democratic republic set up in Germany in 1919 was called the Weimar Republic. Which weakness did it face?

options.text_md: It had no President or parliament
It was ruled directly by Britain and France
It had a single party with a huge majority
Many small parties, so governments were unstable coalitions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Many small parties, so governments were unstable coalitions. Proportional representation produced many parties, and governments were short-lived coalitions. The republic had a President and a parliament (the Reichstag).

questions.stem_md: Article 48 of the Weimar constitution was later misused to weaken democracy. What did it allow?

options.text_md: The army to elect the Chancellor
Citizens to vote directly on every law
The League of Nations to approve German laws
The President to rule by emergency decrees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The President to rule by emergency decrees. Article 48 gave the President emergency powers to govern by decree. From 1930 governments relied on it, which weakened parliament and helped prepare the way for dictatorship.

questions.stem_md: In which year did German money lose almost all its value through hyperinflation?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1923. Hyperinflation peaked in 1923, when the occupation of the Ruhr and the printing of money made the mark almost worthless.

questions.stem_md: How did the Great Depression that began in 1929 help the Nazis?

options.text_md: It made Germany so rich that people wanted change
Mass unemployment and despair made many voters turn to a party promising jobs and strong rule
It ended all political parties except the Nazis
It forced the League of Nations to appoint Hitler

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Mass unemployment and despair made many voters turn to a party promising jobs and strong rule. After 1929 millions lost their jobs, and many Germans turned to the Nazis, who promised work, order and an end to the Versailles settlement. The Depression did not abolish parties.

questions.stem_md: On which date was Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany?

options.text_md: 30 January 1933
28 June 1919
1 September 1939
2 August 1934

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 30 January 1933. President Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933. 2 August 1934 is Hindenburg's death, after which Hitler became Führer.

questions.stem_md: Who appointed Hitler Chancellor in January 1933?

options.text_md: King Victor Emmanuel III
President Paul von Hindenburg
The League of Nations Council
The German people by a direct vote for Chancellor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** President Paul von Hindenburg. The President of the Weimar Republic, Hindenburg, appointed him on the advice of conservative politicians. The Chancellor was not chosen by a direct popular vote.

questions.stem_md: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 allow Hitler's government to do?

options.text_md: Hold free elections every year
Join the League of Nations
Reduce the army to 100,000 men
Make laws without the approval of the Reichstag

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Make laws without the approval of the Reichstag. The Enabling Act let the government make laws without parliament, opening the way to dictatorship. The 100,000 limit was a Versailles term.

questions.stem_md: After which event in August 1934 did Hitler combine the offices of President and Chancellor as Führer?

options.text_md: The death of President Hindenburg
The March on Rome
The Wall Street crash
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The death of President Hindenburg. When Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Hitler merged the two offices and took the title Führer (leader).

questions.stem_md: In the elections of 1932 the Nazi Party became the largest party in the Reichstag. What does this tell us about how Hitler came to power?

options.text_md: The Nazis won more than two-thirds of all votes
Hitler seized power by a successful army revolt in 1932
The Nazis were the largest party but without a majority, and Hitler was then appointed through political deals
Hitler was elected President in 1932

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Nazis were the largest party but without a majority, and Hitler was then appointed through political deals. The Nazis were the largest party but never won an absolute majority in a free election. Hitler became Chancellor by appointment in January 1933, after conservatives believed they could control him.

questions.stem_md: An imagined German teacher in 1923 says her month's salary now buys only a loaf of bread, and people carry banknotes in baskets. Which crisis is she describing?

options.text_md: The Great Depression of 1929
The Enabling Act
Hyperinflation
The Moroccan crisis

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Hyperinflation. Money losing almost all its value in 1923 was hyperinflation. The Depression came after 1929 and caused mass unemployment rather than worthless money.

questions.stem_md: An imagined historian notes that the Nazis won only a small share of the vote in the mid-1920s, although the Treaty of Versailles had been signed in 1919 and the hyperinflation of 1923 had ruined many savers. Their vote grew sharply between 1929 and 1932. Which explanation best fits this timing?

options.text_md: Old resentments mattered more once the Depression brought mass unemployment and the weak coalition governments could not relieve it
The Treaty of Versailles, which was resented from 1919, was the main cause, so the vote should have grown in the mid-1920s
The hyperinflation of 1923 was still ruining savers in 1932, which is why the vote suddenly grew
The Enabling Act of 1933 had already given the Nazis control of elections in 1930

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Old resentments mattered more once the Depression brought mass unemployment and the weak coalition governments could not relieve it. Grievances over the treaty and lost savings existed from the early 1920s but did not by themselves produce a mass vote. The jump came after 1929, when millions lost jobs and unstable governments seemed unable to respond. A grievance present throughout cannot explain a sudden change, the mark was stabilised after 1923, and the Enabling Act came in 1933.

questions.stem_md: An imagined German newspaper of 1930 reports that a government has fallen because the parties could not agree on a budget, and that the President has issued the budget by emergency decree under Article 48. What was the most serious long-term effect of this way of governing?

options.text_md: The decree gave the Nazi Party control of the government in 1930
The decree was illegal, so the President was removed from office
The decree ended the coalition problem and made the republic more democratic
Germans grew used to government by decree instead of by votes in the Reichstag, which made a later dictatorship easier to accept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Germans grew used to government by decree instead of by votes in the Reichstag, which made a later dictatorship easier to accept. Article 48 let the President rule by decree, so when coalitions failed, laws were made without parliament. This weakened the Reichstag and the habit of democratic decision, preparing the way for Hitler. The Nazis did not hold office in 1930, the decree was permitted by the constitution, and decree rule reduced, not increased, democratic control.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined Germans vote for the Nazis in 1932. A retired clerk lost his savings in 1923; a dock worker has been jobless since 1930. Their losses came from different crises. Which statement best explains why both could still make the same choice?

options.text_md: Both losses were caused by the Great Depression, so only one cause is involved
Each had lost faith in a republic that had failed to protect him, and the Nazis promised security to one and work to the other
Both feared a Communist revolution so strongly that their own losses were irrelevant to their votes
Both had belonged to the Nazi Party since 1923 and simply stayed loyal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Each had lost faith in a republic that had failed to protect him, and the Nazis promised security to one and work to the other. The clerk's loss belongs to the hyperinflation of 1923 and the worker's to the Depression after 1929, yet both blamed the republic's governments, and Nazi promises of order, security and jobs appealed to each. The Depression did not cause the 1923 loss, fear of communism was one cause but did not make personal losses irrelevant, and the party was small in 1923.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined Nazi rally in 1932 a speaker promises jobs, an end to the "shameful" peace treaty and protection from the Communists. Which three causes of Nazism do these promises appeal to?

options.text_md: Unemployment, resentment of Versailles and fear of communism
Hyperinflation, the Moroccan crises and imperialism
The mutilated victory, the March on Rome and the corporate state
Collective security, disarmament and arbitration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Unemployment, resentment of Versailles and fear of communism. Jobs answer Depression unemployment, the "shameful" treaty means Versailles, and protection from Communists plays on fear of revolution.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Nazi promise to overturn the Treaty of Versailles won support among many Germans.

**Reason (R):** Many Germans regarded the treaty, with its war-guilt clause, reparations and loss of land, as a national humiliation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: because the treaty was widely resented, a promise to undo it attracted support.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hitler became Chancellor in 1933 because the Nazi Party had won an absolute majority in a free election.

**Reason (R):** The Nazi Party became the largest party in the Reichstag in 1932.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the Nazis never won an absolute majority in a free election; Hitler was appointed by President Hindenburg. R is true: they became the largest party in 1932.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Many middle-class Germans lost faith in the Weimar Republic in the 1920s.

**Reason (R):** The hyperinflation of 1923 wiped out their savings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: people who saw their savings destroyed blamed the republic, which made them open to extreme parties.

questions.stem_md: The article of the Weimar constitution that allowed the President to rule by emergency decree was Article ___.
questions.solution_md: It was Article 48.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Nazi Party won more than half of all votes in a free German election before Hitler became Chancellor.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The Nazis became the largest party in 1932 but never won an absolute majority in a free election; Hitler was appointed Chancellor in January 1933.

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which the Treaty of Versailles helped the rise of Nazism.
questions.solution_md: Two ways.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **war-guilt** clause and **reparations** made Germans feel humiliated and blamed alone.
2. Loss of **land** and limits on the **army** hurt national pride, and the **Nazis** promised to undo the treaty.

questions.stem_md: State two weaknesses of the Weimar Republic that the Nazis were able to exploit.
questions.solution_md: Two weaknesses.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Many parties** meant short-lived **coalition** governments that could not act firmly.
2. **Article 48** let the President rule by **decree**, so parliament was bypassed and democracy weakened.

questions.stem_md: Why did support for the Nazis rise sharply after 1929?
questions.solution_md: Depression and Nazi promises.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Great Depression** threw **millions** of Germans out of work, and the republic seemed helpless.
2. The **Nazis** promised **jobs**, bread and strong leadership, so desperate voters turned to them.

questions.stem_md: What was the Enabling Act of 1933, and why was it important for Hitler?
questions.solution_md: Meaning and importance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Passed in **March 1933**, it let Hitler's government make **laws** without the **Reichstag**.
2. It ended parliamentary control and became the **legal basis** of his **dictatorship**.

questions.stem_md: How did the fear of communism help Hitler come to power?
questions.solution_md: Two points.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Industrialists**, landowners and the **middle class** feared a **communist revolution** and saw the Nazis as a barrier against it.
2. **Conservative** politicians advised **Hindenburg** to appoint Hitler in **1933**, hoping to use him against the left.

questions.stem_md: Give three causes of the rise of Nazism in Germany, with one fact for each.
questions.solution_md: Three causes, each with a fact.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Treaty of Versailles:** the **war-guilt** clause, reparations and lost land were seen as a humiliation.
2. **Economic crisis:** **hyperinflation** in **1923** and the **Great Depression** after **1929** brought ruin and mass unemployment.
3. **Weak Weimar Republic:** unstable **coalitions** and rule by decree under **Article 48** made democracy look helpless.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the rise of Nazism in Germany.

(i) How did the Treaty of Versailles create resentment that the Nazis could use? **[3]**
(ii) Explain the weaknesses of the Weimar Republic. **[3]**
(iii) How did the economic crises of 1923 and 1929 help the Nazis gain support? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Versailles; Weimar weaknesses; economic crises.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The treaty made Germany accept **war guilt** and pay **reparations**. Germany lost **land** and **colonies**, and its army was cut to **100,000**. It was a **dictated** peace, so many Germans felt humiliated, and the **Nazis** promised to tear it up.

(ii) The republic had **many parties**, so governments were unstable **coalitions**. Many Germans linked it with defeat and the treaty. **Article 48** let the President rule by **decree**, and from **1930** governments relied on it, weakening parliament.

(iii) In **1923** **hyperinflation** made money worthless and wiped out the **savings** of the middle class. After **1929** the **Great Depression** threw **millions** out of work. Desperate people lost faith in democracy. The **Nazis** promised **jobs**, order and national revival, and in **1932** they became the **largest party** in the **Reichstag**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about how Hitler gained and secured power.

(i) Explain how Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933. **[3]**
(ii) What was the Enabling Act, and how did it change Germany's government? **[3]**
(iii) Describe how Hitler became Führer in 1934 and explain why the period 1933–34 is called the consolidation of the Nazi dictatorship. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Appointment; Enabling Act; Führer and consolidation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Nazis became the **largest party** in the **Reichstag** in **1932** but had no majority. Conservative politicians believed they could control Hitler and persuaded **President Hindenburg** to appoint him **Chancellor** on **30 January 1933**.

(ii) Passed in **March 1933**, the **Enabling Act** allowed the government to make **laws** without the **Reichstag**. Parliament lost its power, other parties were soon **banned**, and Germany became a **one-party state**.

(iii) When **Hindenburg** died on **2 August 1934**, Hitler combined the offices of **President** and **Chancellor** and took the title **Führer**; the **army** swore loyalty to him personally. In just over a year he had moved from appointed Chancellor to **dictator**, removing **opposition**, **trade unions** and a free **press**, so these years mark the consolidation of his power.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **1923:** hyperinflation made German money almost worthless. **1932:** the Nazis became the largest party in the **Reichstag**, though without a majority. **1933:** Hitler was appointed **Chancellor** in January, and the **Enabling Act** was passed in March.

(ii) **11 years** (1933 − 1922). **Mussolini** came to power first, after the March on Rome in **1922**; Hitler followed in **1933**.

(iii) In **1923** **hyperinflation** destroyed the **savings** of the middle class, and many families blamed the republic and lost faith in democracy. After the **Depression** began in **1929**, factories closed and **unemployment** rose to millions, while weak governments could do little. Desperate voters turned to a party that promised jobs and order, so by **1932** the Nazis were the **largest party**. In **1933** Hitler took power and quickly set up a **dictatorship**.

questions.stem_md: Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany are both called totalitarian states. What does this mean?

options.text_md: Power was shared among many parties and free courts
The state tried to control every part of people's lives, with one party and no opposition allowed
The states were governed by the League of Nations
Each region ruled itself without a central government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The state tried to control every part of people's lives, with one party and no opposition allowed. A totalitarian state controls political, economic and social life under one party, banning opposition and free expression.

questions.stem_md: Both regimes presented their leader as all-wise and always right, with his image everywhere. This feature is called

options.text_md: collective security
parliamentary democracy
the cult of the leader
separation of powers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the cult of the leader. Glorifying the single leader, Il Duce or the Führer, was the cult of the leader. The other options belong to democracies or the League.

questions.stem_md: Which view of war was common to both Fascism and Nazism?

options.text_md: War was to be avoided by settling every dispute through the League
Armies should be abolished
Only colonies should fight wars
War was glorified as a way to make the nation strong and great

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** War was glorified as a way to make the nation strong and great. Both glorified war and military strength as signs of national greatness and built up their armed forces.

questions.stem_md: Which political idea did both Fascism and Nazism strongly oppose?

options.text_md: Nationalism
Militarism
Dictatorship
Communism

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Communism. Both were bitterly anti-communist and won support by promising to crush communism. They themselves were nationalist, militarist dictatorships.

questions.stem_md: Which feature was central to Nazism but much less important in Italian Fascism in its early years?

options.text_md: A one-party state
The use of propaganda
A racial doctrine of a superior race, with hatred of Jews (antisemitism)
Opposition to communism

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A racial doctrine of a superior race, with hatred of Jews (antisemitism). Nazism placed race at its centre and persecuted Jews, leading to the Holocaust. A one-party state, propaganda and anti-communism were shared by both.

questions.stem_md: Why did both regimes organise boys and girls into official youth movements?

options.text_md: To prepare them for free elections
To train the young in loyalty to the leader and the party from childhood
To teach them to criticise the government
To send them to study abroad

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To train the young in loyalty to the leader and the party from childhood. Youth organisations (such as the Hitler Youth) shaped the young to obey the leader, accept the party's ideas and be ready for military service.

questions.stem_md: An imagined poster of 1936 shows a giant portrait of the national leader above cheering crowds, with a caption saying he is never wrong. A student says: "This proves that most citizens admired him." Which reply is best?

options.text_md: The poster shows what the regime wanted people to believe; with no free press, other evidence is needed to know what citizens really thought
The student is right, because a regime could not print a poster that most citizens disliked
The student is wrong, because posters are produced by governments and so are useless as evidence of anything
The student is right, because the crowds in the picture show how many people attended the rallies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The poster shows what the regime wanted people to believe; with no free press, other evidence is needed to know what citizens really thought. A poster is evidence of the regime's propaganda and of the cult of the leader, but under a one-party state with no free press it cannot show real public opinion. It is useful evidence for what the regime wanted, so it is not worthless, and a drawn crowd is not a count of attendance.

questions.stem_md: An imagined 1937 report on a state youth group in a dictatorship notes that members wear uniforms, meet after school, practise marching, and sing songs praising the leader, while all other youth clubs have been closed. Which detail is the strongest evidence that the aim was loyalty to the leader rather than leisure?

options.text_md: The uniforms, since only political groups wear uniforms
The songs praising the leader, together with the closing of every other youth club
The meetings after school, since leisure groups never meet at that time
The marching, since marching is never part of a sports club

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The songs praising the leader, together with the closing of every other youth club. Songs of praise show what the group taught, and closing all rival clubs shows that children were allowed no other loyalty. Uniforms, after-school meetings and drill also occur in sports and scouting groups, so alone they do not show a political aim.

questions.stem_md: An imagined editor in 1934 is told that every article must be checked by a government office and that criticising the leader is a crime. Which common feature does this show?

options.text_md: A free press protected by courts
Rule by the League of Nations
Separation of powers
Suppression of civil liberties and control of the press

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Suppression of civil liberties and control of the press. Censorship and punishment of criticism show the suppression of free speech and the press under both regimes.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Both Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany allowed only one political party.

**Reason (R):** Both Fascism and Nazism believed in parliamentary democracy and free elections.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: each became a one-party state. R is false: both rejected parliamentary democracy and free elections.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Both regimes made heavy use of propaganda through newspapers, radio, films and rallies.

**Reason (R):** Mussolini became Prime Minister of Italy in 1922.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Propaganda was used to win and keep mass support and to glorify the leader; the date of Mussolini's appointment does not explain it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A racial doctrine and hatred of Jews were central to Nazism, while in Italian Fascism the state rather than race was the central idea in its early years.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Nazism was built on racial ideas and antisemitism; Italian Fascism placed the state at the centre (Italy adopted anti-Jewish laws only later, in 1938).

questions.stem_md: Match each term from the rise of the dictatorships with its meaning.

options.text_md: Il Duce
Führer
Blackshirts
Enabling Act

match_right.text_md: Law of 1933 letting the government rule without parliament
Title of Mussolini as leader of Italy

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Il Duce and Führer both mean "the leader"; the Blackshirts were Mussolini's squads; the Enabling Act of 1933 opened the way to Hitler's dictatorship.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events from the rise of the dictatorships in the order in which they happened.

options.text_md: Fascist movement founded at Milan
Hitler takes the title Führer
Beginning of the Great Depression
March on Rome
Hitler appointed Chancellor
Hyperinflation in Germany

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (a) → (d) → (f) → (c) → (e) → (b). Fascist movement (1919), March on Rome (1922), hyperinflation (1923), Great Depression (1929), Hitler Chancellor (1933), Führer (1934).

questions.stem_md: State two features common to the ideologies of Fascism and Nazism.
questions.solution_md: Two common features.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **totalitarian one-party state** in which no opposition or free elections were allowed.
2. **Extreme nationalism** with the **glorification of war** and a **cult of the leader**.

questions.stem_md: Explain one important difference between Nazism and Italian Fascism.
questions.solution_md: Race versus state.

answer.model_answer_md: Nazism made **race** its central idea, claiming a superior race and spreading **antisemitism**, which led to the persecution of **Jews** and the **Holocaust**. Italian Fascism placed the **state** at the centre.

questions.stem_md: An imagined radio in 1935 plays only speeches praising the government. Explain how such propaganda helped both dictatorships.
questions.solution_md: Two effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Constant **propaganda** on radio, in films and **newspapers** made people believe the **leader** was always right.
2. With no **free press**, opposing views were hidden, so the regime kept **mass support**.

questions.stem_md: Describe three similarities between the ideologies of Fascism and Nazism.
questions.solution_md: Three similarities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **One-party rule:** both set up **totalitarian** states, banned other parties and ended free elections.
2. **Extreme nationalism and militarism:** both glorified **war** and promised national **greatness**.
3. **Cult of the leader:** **Il Duce** and the **Führer** were shown as all-wise, supported by **propaganda** and **youth organisations**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the ideologies of Fascism and Nazism.

(i) What is a totalitarian state? Give two ways in which both regimes controlled people's lives. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the attitude of both ideologies to nationalism, war and communism. **[3]**
(iii) Describe two further similarities and one major difference between the two ideologies. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Totalitarianism; nationalism, war and communism; further similarities and a difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **totalitarian** state seeks to control every part of life through **one party**. Both regimes banned other **parties** and **trade unions**, and used **censorship** and **secret police** to silence critics.

(ii) Both preached **extreme nationalism**, placing the nation above the individual. They **glorified war** and built up armed forces. Both were fiercely **anti-communist** and won the support of property owners by promising to crush communism.

(iii) **Similarities:** a **cult of the leader** (Il Duce and the Führer) and the use of **propaganda** and **youth organisations** to win loyalty. **Difference:** Nazism made **race** central, with **antisemitism** that led to the persecution of Jews and the **Holocaust**; Italian Fascism stressed the **state** above all.

(ii) In both countries **landowners**, **industrialists** and the **middle class** feared a **communist revolution**. My brother came back from the mountains three years ago and still has no work. Bread costs twice what it did before the war. Last spring the metal workers held the factories for weeks and hung red flags from the gates. Now young men in black shirts march through the square, and the mill owners are said to pay them. My neighbour says the government in Rome changes so often that nobody remembers the minister's name.

questions.passage_md:
**Letter from an imagined Berlin shopkeeper to her sister in Munich, 1932**

Three years ago the shop had six assistants; now there is only me. Half the men on our street stand in the queue at the labour office each morning. Ten years ago we lost our savings when money became paper; now we may lose the shop. The parties in the Reichstag argue and the Chancellor rules by emergency orders. A man at the corner hands out leaflets promising work for everyone and an end to the treaty that shamed us. Many neighbours say they will vote for his party.

children.stem_md: Which crisis of "ten years ago" made money "become paper"?

answer.model_answer_md: The **hyperinflation** of **1923**.

children.stem_md: Which crisis explains the queue at the labour office in 1932?

answer.model_answer_md: The **Great Depression** that began in **1929**, causing mass **unemployment**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which party do the leaflets most likely come from, and which two of its promises appeal to the shopkeeper's neighbours?

answer.model_answer_md: The **Nazi Party**. It promises **work** for the unemployed and to **overturn the Treaty of Versailles**, which many Germans saw as a humiliation.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which weakness of the Weimar Republic does the sentence about the Reichstag show, and why did it matter?

answer.model_answer_md: Quarrelling **parties** could not form stable governments, so the Chancellor ruled by **decree** under **Article 48**; democracy looked **helpless**, and people turned to extremists.

In Rome and in Munich the walls carry the same kind of poster: one man's face, larger than life. In both cities children march in uniform after school.
